title: From Seasonal to Persistent Heat Stress: Global Warming-Level Transitions Across Dairy Cattle Systems
content: Heat stress is already common in dairy production, but global projections have mostly been reported for fixed future periods or as threshold exceedances. These approaches do not show when production areas move from episodic exposure to persistent stress, nor whether daytime exposure is accompanied by a loss of nocturnal recovery. We combined bias-adjusted daily NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 data from five models with a dairy-cattle spatial proxy derived from GLW3 total cattle and national FAOSTAT milk-animal shares. Daily mean, minimum and maximum temperature-humidity index (THI) were reconstructed and evaluated against ERA5 hourly data at 24 dairy-region sites. We then quantified stress frequency, no-recovery nights, annual THI degree-hours, regime transitions and conditional changes in the climatological stress window at global warming levels of +1.5, +2 and +3°C relative to 1850–1900. The daily reconstruction reproduced mean, minimum and maximum THI with correlations above 0.998. In the 1995–2014 reference period, the dairy-cattle proxy was exposed to maximum THI values of at least 72 on 61.9% of days and to minimum THI values of at least 70 on 27.3% of nights. These proportions reached 69.6% and 38.6%, respectively, at +3°C, while annual heat load increased from 23,894 to 38,116 THI degree-hours. At +3°C, 24.2% of the dairy-cattle proxy occurred in grid cells undergoing an upward modal heat-stress regime transition, and the share exposed to a quasi-permanent regime increased from 36.8% to 46.9%. In cells with complete five-model phenological support, stress-window onset advanced by 18.3 days, its end shifted 17.0 days later, and its span lengthened by 35.3 days. These results distinguish increasing nocturnal and cumulative heat load in already warm regions from seasonal expansion and regime change in cooler dairy-production regions. This distinction is relevant to adaptation because the feasibility and resource requirements of short-term heat relief differ substantially from those of sustained cooling and recovery management.
